quizzes.title: The 90 Per Dollar Breach
quizzes.passage: The Indian rupee crossed the 90 per US dollar mark in 2025, a development that marked a notable moment in the currency's recent trajectory. Over the course of the year, the rupee had weakened against the dollar, and the slide carried it below that level. India's financial markets experienced heightened volatility as a result. The fall came even as the economy showed strong growth and inflation stayed low, which nonetheless raised concerns about the country's broader macroeconomic stability. Market analysts attributed the rupee's weakness to a combination of global and domestic factors. Investors had been watching several developments closely through the year. The 90 level was noticed widely across markets, and the move past it drew attention from participants in the currency market. The breach was reported as part of the December 2025 current affairs coverage of the economy. As the currency continues to navigate these headwinds, policymakers and investors alike will be closely monitoring global financial conditions, external trade developments and domestic economic indicators to assess the rupee's stability in the months ahead. Coverage of the episode has drawn attention to the currency's movement across the year and to the mix of developments that shaped it. The breach has been discussed as a moment worth tracking in the months that follow.

questions.q: What GDP growth rate did the booklet cite for India at the time of the rupee's fall?
questions.explanation: The booklet cites India's strong 8.2% GDP growth alongside the rupee's fall.

questions.q: When the rupee crosses 90 per US dollar, which type of orders can be activated?
questions.explanation: The booklet says crossing 90 can activate buy-stop orders.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Crossing the 90 level can intensify downward momentum in the rupee.
Reason (R): Crossing 90 can activate buy-stop orders.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: Buy-stop orders triggered at 90 are what intensify the downward momentum, so R explains A.

questions.q: According to the booklet, what does the 2025 breach of 90 per dollar reflect?
options: A deliberate devaluation by the RBI
questions.explanation: The booklet says the breach reflects the cumulative effect of pressures that built over time.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the rupee's weakness in 2025:
I. Delays in the initial tranche of the India-US trade agreement were among the factors behind the weakness.
II. Investors had been anticipating the initial tranche of the India-US trade agreement.
III. Crossing 90 per dollar reduces the chance of buy-stop orders being activated.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II match the booklet, while III reverses its point that crossing 90 can activate buy-stop orders.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about the 2025 rupee breach are correct?
I. Market analysts cited sustained strength in the US dollar as a factor behind the weakness.
II. The breach is described as having been caused by a single disruptive event.
III. Strong growth and low inflation were reported at the time.
questions.explanation: Statements I and III are in the booklet, while II contradicts its description of cumulative pressures.

questions.q: What kind of importance does the booklet attribute to the 90 level for traders?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the 90 level holds substantial psychological importance for traders.

quizzes.title: Depreciation or Devaluation
quizzes.passage: When a currency's value falls, financial news commonly uses two terms: depreciation and devaluation. Both describe a lower value for the currency against foreign currencies, yet the terms are not identical, and the distinction matters when a currency's movement is discussed. In recent months, the rupee's decline against the US dollar has been described mainly in terms of depreciation. Analysts have pointed to the sustained strength of the dollar as one of the wider developments in the background, alongside uncertainty about trade ties between India and the United States. Understanding the two terms helps readers follow economic debates. A fall in a currency's value can be discussed in different ways, depending on what is being described. The rupee's movement in 2025 was reported in the December 2025 current affairs coverage of the economy, and the booklet explains the vocabulary used in that coverage. Readers of current affairs should therefore look at the context in which a currency's value changes before deciding which term applies. The terms appear often in news coverage of the rupee, which makes them useful to recognise when reading about the economy. The rupee's decline is one example of how these terms are used in practice. Both terms are used in the booklet's economy section, which explains each one in turn.

questions.q: Under which exchange rate system does devaluation occur?
questions.explanation: The booklet says devaluation happens under fixed or pegged exchange rate systems.

questions.q: Which of the following does the booklet list as a cause of rupee depreciation?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists the current account deficit among the causes of depreciation, along with FPI outflows, inflation and global shocks.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Devaluation is carried out as a policy tool rather than through market forces.
Reason (R): Devaluation happens when the government or RBI deliberately reduces the currency's value.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The booklet defines devaluation as a deliberate reduction by the government or RBI, which is why it is a policy action.

questions.q: What does the booklet say devaluation is used for, as a policy tool?
options: Boosting exports and reducing the deficit
questions.explanation: The booklet calls devaluation a policy tool to boost exports and reduce the deficit.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Depreciation   ->   A. Caused by market forces, capital flows and external shocks
II. Devaluation   ->   B. Deliberate reduction by the government or RBI
III. Fixed or pegged system   ->   C. Where devaluation happens
IV. Floating system   ->   D. Where depreciation happens
questions.explanation: Depreciation is driven by market forces, devaluation is a deliberate act, and each exchange system goes with its matching term.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Depreciation can be caused by a rise in inflation and a larger current account deficit.
II. Devaluation happens under a floating exchange rate system.
III. Devaluation is a market-driven fall in the currency's value.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement I matches the booklet's causes of depreciation, while II and III describe depreciation rather than devaluation.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about the rupee are correct?
I. Depreciation happens under floating or managed-floating systems.
II. Devaluation can be caused by global shocks.
III. Depreciation can be triggered by policy uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Statements I and III match the booklet, while II is wrong because devaluation is a deliberate policy action.

questions.q: Along with the government, which central bank is named as deliberately reducing a currency's value in devaluation? (short form)

questions.q: Which abbreviation, standing for a current account measure, is named as a cause of depreciation? (short form)

questions.explanation: The booklet lists external shocks as one of the causes of depreciation.

quizzes.title: Effects of a Weaker Rupee
quizzes.passage: A currency's fall against foreign currencies has effects that run in more than one direction through an economy. Some effects are favourable, while others add costs to households, businesses and the government. The booklet presents these consequences under two headings, positive and negative, which helps readers weigh gains against burdens. Trade, government budgets and companies are all touched by such changes, and the effects can be felt in different ways by different groups. In 2025 the rupee's weakness drew close attention in financial markets, even though India's economy showed strong growth at the time. The booklet also discusses measures aimed at stabilising the rupee. The booklet's account therefore covers both sides of the picture, so readers can see how each consequence is grouped under its heading and how the two headings relate to one another in the economy section. Under the positive heading, the booklet lists effects that make some parts of the economy more competitive. Under the negative heading, it lists effects that raise costs for households, businesses and the government. The booklet also explains the reasons behind several of these effects, so each one can be understood in context rather than in isolation. The rupee's path in 2025 is one example of how such effects appear in practice, since its weakness was discussed alongside India's growth.

questions.q: Which group gets a more favourable exchange rate when sending money home during rupee depreciation?
questions.explanation: The booklet says NRIs send money at a more favourable exchange rate when the rupee weakens.

questions.q: What does a weaker rupee make costlier for companies that hold dollar-denominated loans?
questions.explanation: The booklet says companies with dollar-denominated loans face higher repayment and interest costs.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A weaker rupee can encourage domestic manufacturing.
Reason (R): Expensive imports encourage local production.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
questions.explanation: Expensive imports pushing local production is the mechanism through which depreciation encourages domestic manufacturing.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Higher subsidy burden   ->   A. Fertiliser imports become costlier
II. Boost to exports   ->   B. Indian goods become cheaper globally
III. Capital flight risk   ->   C. Weak rupee reduces investor confidence
IV. Lower consumer purchasing power   ->   D. Costlier essential imports
questions.explanation: Each consequence matches the item it is linked to in the booklet, such as costlier fertiliser imports driving a larger subsidy burden.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. A weaker rupee makes Indian goods more expensive for foreign buyers.
II. A weaker rupee can widen the current account deficit.
III. A weaker rupee can raise imported inflation in crude oil and fertilisers.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements II and III match the booklet, while I reverses its point that Indian goods become cheaper abroad.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements are correct?
I. A weaker rupee lowers the subsidy bill on fertilisers.
II. NRIs get a more favourable exchange rate on remittances.
III. A weaker rupee encourages domestic manufacturing as imports become expensive.
questions.explanation: Statements II and III match the booklet, while I is wrong because a weaker rupee raises the subsidy burden.

questions.q: Which of these is a negative impact of rupee depreciation?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists a higher subsidy burden under the negative impacts of depreciation.

questions.q: What is the name the booklet gives to the rise in prices caused by costlier imports? (two words)

questions.q: Which subsidy-linked import becomes costlier, leading to a larger subsidy bill? (one word)

questions.q: What is the risk called when a weak rupee reduces investor confidence? (two words)

questions.q: Which sector does a weak rupee encourage, as expensive imports push local production? (two words)
